title: Multi-AZ PrivateLink failover + DNS & KV-cache impact postmortem
summary: Postmortem-style deep dive on a cross-AZ PrivateLink failover that surfaced DNS resolution and KV cache warmup issues. Discussed NAT fallback, route table design, ENI limits, and mitigation patterns to preserve latency SLOs. Agreed on tests, runbook updates, and follow-up benchmarking windows.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 72 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Rita (Redwood SE), Samir (Cerulean Lead Infra), Diana (Cerulean SRE), Kenji (Cerulean Security)

Summary (auto): quick timeline of failover, observed latency/regression windows, root causes suspected (DNS TTL & resolver config, KV cache cold start due to rehoming), and remediation options including NAT fallback, route table sticky ENI attach, and pre-warming.

[00:00] Alex: okay hi everyone thanks for joining for the postmortem, i'm alex from redwood inference, rita is our se who dug into the runtime traces, we got the cerulean folks on the call, maybe quick intros?
[00:18] Samir: yeah thanks alex, i'm samir, i run infra for cerulean, diana and kenji are on security and sres, we had a production blip yesterday where latency spiked for about five to seven minutes and some requests fell back to the hosted variant.
[00:30] Diana: hi all, the p99 jumped from 210ms to about 1.1s and error rate nudged up, so we throttled a bit.
[00:42] Rita: we pulled the runtime logs — packets looked fine, but we saw a KV hit rate drop from 92% to 34% coincident with the cross-az privatelink failover event, which then increased token generation time.
[01:05] Kenji: from security side we noticed no auth failures, but egress path changed briefly which triggered our logging and some policy alerts; we manually acknowledged.

[01:30] Alex: can you run through the sequence you saw in cloudwatch / VPC flow? samir?
[01:40] Samir: yeah so here's what happened — AZ A's endpoint ENI suddenly lost reachability to the customer's appliance (we think it was a hardware flake), AWS re-homed the privatelink to AZ B; the endpoint IP changed, route table didn't need updates, but our internal resolver had an unresolved cache and pointed some nodes at the old IP for ~40s because our OS TTL and dnsmasq settings were aggressive.
[02:10] Diana: yep i pulled the node-level /etc/resolv.conf and dnsmasq logs — we had negative cache and long re-query intervals, so a subset of inference hosts kept hitting the old path and fell back to the Redwood hosted fallback.
[02:30] Rita: the critical piece is KV cache — our runtime keeps per-host local KV that maps model prefixes and precomputed LM context. When a node falls back to hosted or is reattached, the local KV is invalidated or cold. We saw a miss storm where many requests missed the local KV and forced full KV reconstruction, which produced additional latency and increased token generation time.
[03:05] Alex: couple of clarifying q's — what was the scale? how many nodes/ENIs were impacted and what is your subnet sizing?
[03:15] Samir: affected about 18 of our inference pods across two ASGs, each in a /26; subnet had spare IPs but we were close to ENI attach limits on the instance type. The re-homing forced transient reconnection while ENIs detached and reattached which touched the kube-proxy rules briefly.
[03:45] Kenji: is this an ENI quota problem or an artifact of the PrivateLink design?
[03:52] Rita: it's more of a combination — PrivateLink failover itself is expected to reassign endpoints, that's fine. The unexpected part was the resolver and per-host KV interplay. If the resolver immediately returned new endpoint IPs then hosts would reconnect and warm kv quickly. But because some hosts were stuck on stale DNS answers they retried via fallback rules.
[04:15] Alex: right — and fallback to hosted is explicitly configured to preserve availability, but that moves compute off-prem and increases latency due to network hop to hosted region and also causes KV mismatch. So we need to reduce the window where fallback happens and improve warmup.

[04:35] [Small crosstalk] Diana: also want to note that customers using split-horizon DNS for private endpoints can exacerbate things if the resolver chain isn't consistent across AZs.
[04:50] Rita: good point — and we saw that cerulean has an internal resolver chain: node -> dnsmasq -> vpc-resolver -> rt resolver. The dnsmasq negative cache TTL was set to 300s, that was too long.

[05:10] Samir: so action items on our side include lowering negative caching and standardizing resolvers across AZs. but rita, from redwood side what are the mitigation knobs?
[05:22] Rita: couple of runtime-level mitigations: 1) KV prefetch on attach — when a node sees an endpoint reattach event, trigger a background pre-warm of top-k prefixes; 2) sticky routing — keep existing connections alive for a brief drain window instead of immediate failover to hosted; 3) smarter fallback thresholds — use a combination of DNS failure count + KV miss rate to decide to fallback.
[05:52] Alex: can you expand on pre-warm script steps and any required permissions?
[06:00] Rita: sure — script uses the same internal API we use for pre-warm in Dedicated, it needs to call the local runtime endpoint on 127.0.0.1:12000 with an auth token scoped to infra role. It issues synthetic requests for the top N prompt prefixes to prime the kv. No KMS changes required, but the token needs rotate policy. We'll share sample snippet.
[06:30] Samir: ok that's good. what about NAT fallback? we have a constrained security policy that prevents wide-open egress; we prefer privatelink only.
[06:42] Alex: understood. NAT fallback is an option only when PrivateLink is unavailable and customer allows egress via NAT gateway or VPC egress proxy. Mechanically, swapping to NAT keeps requests on Cerulean’s infra but still changes pathing for endpoints that rely on service-constructed DNS names — you'll need to map route tables and ensure your NACLs allow the egress. It's a more permissive posture though.
[07:05] Kenji: security concern — nat fallback may send hashed request metadata to an external IP if hosted path used; we need to validate what gets sent and if KMS/HSM keys stay local.
[07:18] Rita: for our hosted fallback we route only inference request payloads; we do not store customer keys. If keys are client-side for decryption, they remain local. We'll document exact headers and IP ranges.
[07:35] Alex: another element was ENI attach concurrency — you said instance type hits attach limits?
[07:42] Samir: yes M6i-family with default ENI limits, when many endpoints rehome concurrently you can hit per-instance ENI attach detach rates and that adds 10-20s of jitter.
[07:55] Rita: mitigation: increase instance type ENI capacity (bigger instance) or shift endpoints to fewer nodes or use secondary ENI pool in the same AZ. Also stagger endpoint reconnection using exponential backoff to avoid thundering herd on the kube-proxy.
[08:20] Diana: any quantization/batching effects during the failover? did model execution change behavior?
[08:28] Rita: yes — because of KV misses we moved from short-circuit path to slower quantized decode path where cache misses force recompute of key/value tensors. That increased per-token compute by about ~30% for the affected requests; batching was slightly less efficient because hosts weren't grouped by warm prefixes, so effective throughput dropped.
[08:55] Alex: rita, can you quantify p50/p95 token generation delta during the window?
[09:02] Rita: p50 went from 45ms to 70ms per token, p95 jumped from 120ms to 420ms for affected nodes. That matches the p99 from diana's view.
[09:18] Samir: are there kernel-level tunables or GPU scheduler knobs we should change?
[09:24] Rita: not really kernel-level, but runtime queue sizing and batch window can be slightly adjusted — you can lower batch accumulation timeout to favor latency during degraded warm-up windows; that reduces throughput but keeps p95 lower. We can ship config change toggles per-workload.
[09:44] Diana: so tradeoff matrix is: lower batch windows => better latency under cold but worse throughput / cost. Need to decide by workload.
[09:52] Alex: agreed — for payment auth we want latency primacy; for background embedding jobs we want throughput. We should classify route-level SLOs in routing config.

[10:10] [Pause — someone paging another doc link]
[10:20] Rita: we also observed DNS TTL behavior and iptables conntrack entries — some conntrack entries prevented reestablishing clean sockets and caused long tails. Clearing conntrack helped faster reconnection. So adding a conntrack stale cleanup during endpoint change helps.
[10:45] Kenji: can you list the exact observability metrics we should monitor to detect this early?
[10:52] Rita: yes — KV cache hit rate per-host, endpoint DNS resolution latency and failure count, ENI attach/detach event rate, fallback-to-hosted count, per-token p95 latency, batch size histogram, and conntrack count spikes. We'll add recommended thresholds.
[11:15] Alex: we'll share a dashboard that combines these signals. any additional concerns about internal split-horizon resolver anomalies?
[11:24] Samir: i want to double-check our resolver hierarchy; i think one of our AZ-resolvers had an outdated zone file. We'll audit and sync.

[11:40] Diana: timeline for remediation? ideally we do small config changes first: lower dns negative cache, add conntrack cleanup hook, and runtime prewarm. Then schedule a staged failover test.
[11:55] Alex: sounds good. Rita, can you outline the staging test plan?
[12:02] Rita: plan: 1) pick a single AZ in staging with mirrored infra, 2) cause endpoint rehome via simulated flake (we have scripts), 3) measure KV hit rate, per-token latency, batch sizes in 5s windows, 4) exercise fallback policy by toggling host fallback knob, 5) capture packet-trace and logs and compare to baseline. We'll join for the window.
[12:30] Samir: how long to prepare? we can mirror infra in 2 days. queue se for the run.
[12:40] Alex: i'll slot rita and myself for the test; samir to propose a time.

[12:52] Kenji: on the security notes — need an updated runbook entry for incident response when endpoint rehomes; i want explicit steps for verifying KMS locality, logging assertions, and a roll-back flow.
[13:05] Rita: we'll include explicit checks: 1) confirm resolver mapping to private ip, 2) verify KV hit rate recovered above 85% within 120s, 3) if not, escalate to manual failover of route tables.
[13:25] Diana: is manual route table failover documented? we've never done that live for inference endpoints.
[13:32] Alex: we have a runbook snippet, i'll send link. it's basically set of route priorities and a small script to move a route to an alternative NAT in the same AZ. note this is invasive so prefer DNS/resolve fixes and pre-warm first.

[13:55] Samir: small question — when you say 'KV warm' is that per-pod or per-node?
[14:03] Rita: per-runtime instance (per pod in your case). so when pod dies and is recreated on another node the new pod starts cold. If a pod temporarily loses connectivity the on-disk KV may stay cached depending on your container restart semantics. We recommend sticky scheduling for critical pods.
[14:25] Diana: any recommended subnet sizing rules? you mentioned /26 was used.
[14:31] Rita: for high-availability with privatelink endpoints, we recommend at least /24 per AZ for inference clusters if you plan large scale or frequent endpoint rehome to avoid IP scarcity and ENI attach pressure. If using smaller subnets, plan for ENI attach quotas and test attach rates.

[14:55] Alex: ok let's capture explicit deliverables now — and then quick recap.
[15:02] Samir: recap — lower negative DNS TTLs, run staging failover with redwood, get pre-warm script, test conntrack cleanup, and decide if NAT fallback allowed.
[15:15] Alex: i'll share runbook + route table diffs: https://redwood.app/privatelink-runbook (placeholder) and https://redwood.app/kvcache-warmup-sample (placeholder). Rita will share warmup script in git gist.
[15:30] Rita: i'll also attach a sample Grafana dashboard and alert thresholds.
[15:38] Kenji: i'll circulate SOC items that need runbook evidence and we'll update our incident playbooks.

[15:50] Diana: anything else on batching/quantization we should tune now?
[15:55] Rita: for immediate change toggles: reduce batch accumulation timeout from 25ms to 8ms for auth path routes, increase per-shard worker threads to allow parallel pre-warm, and enable kv-preload on attach. We'll provide a patch and a toggle flag.

[16:12] Alex: sound good. thanks everyone. we'll check-in after the staging test and plan production rollouts.

End recap (auto):
- Root cause: PrivateLink rehome + long negative DNS cache + ENI attach jitter => KV cold starts => increased per-token latency and fallback to hosted.
- Mitigations: lower dns negative TTLs, add runtime KV pre-warm, conntrack cleanup hook, consider NAT fallback policy if allowed, and increase subnet/ENI capacity or stagger endpoint reconnections.
- Next steps: run staging failover with Redwood SEs present, share runbook and scripts, update SOC/incident playbooks.

References/Links shared during call:
- PrivateLink runbook (placeholder): https://redwood.app/privatelink-runbook
